title: PureLogs Malware Uses BYOVD, AMSI Bypass and Process Hollowing to Evade Detection
content_md: A phishing campaign targeting recipients with Japanese- and Korean-language emails used fake damaged-product complaints to deliver PureLogs and PureRAT . Researchers observed the activity between July and August 2026. Although the final malware belonged to the same families, the attackers changed the loaders between samples, complicating detection based on file hashes alone. The emails claimed that a delivered product was damaged and asked the recipient to review an unboxing video or inspection document before arranging an exchange or refund. Links led to pages imitating document-sharing or video-viewing services. Visitors were told the file was too large to preview and were prompted to download a ZIP archive. PureLogs Evades Detection with BYOVD The pages offered Vietnamese, English, Chinese, Japanese, and Korean language options. They also hid the download button from mobile visitors. These features suggest the campaign was designed for multiple audiences, though the researchers directly observed Japanese- and Korean-language emails. Fake page impersonating a document-sharing service (Source: itochuci) The ZIP archives varied, but commonly paired an executable disguised with a document-style name or double extension with a malicious DLL . In some cases, the executable was a legitimate Microsoft-signed Excel binary used to load the DLL. Other archives included a Python interpreter or a Lenovo-signed driver.
